extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political economy; economists and people interested in industrial/manufacturing organization
extracted.subtask_short: division of labour and raw materials
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level textbook guidance on how to measure value across time, the role of raw materials versus labour in manufactured goods, and the principles and practical effects of the division of labour (illustrated by pin-making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of value for intertemporal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Malthus has proposed for this purpose to consider a day's labour of an agricultural labourer as the unit to which all value should be referred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compare the value of the same manufactured good at different times, find how many days' labour the good would have purchased at those times and compare. Agricultural labour is selected because it exists in all countries, employs many persons, and requires little prior instruction. The author also suggests possibly combining agricultural labour with trades requiring moderate skill (blacksmith, carpenter) to obtain a more constant average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsistence-food estimate as an adjunct measure
rubrics_metrics.description: An estimate of the quantity of the food on which the labourer usually subsists, compared with the quantity which his daily wages will purchase, is a useful additional element in judging value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not essential, comparing wages to the cost/quantity of the labourer's usual food adds information when using labour as a unit of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of middle-men in price formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a class of middle-men between small producers and merchants is frequently advantageous, but when numerous they may enhance price without equivalent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middle-men can be helpful at certain manufacture stages but can cease to confer advantage. Example: 'brass-plate coal-merchants' supply five-sixths of London public and receive commissions that constitute loss to the consumer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'raw material' stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Many substances in a certain stage of manufacture are called 'raw material' — e.g., iron rendered malleable is a raw material for many tools; in this stage only a moderate quantity of labour has been expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing the proportions in which raw material and labour unite to constitute value of manufactured products is an important subject of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative contributions of material and labour in specific manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: In some products the raw material constitutes the greater share of value (e.g., gold-leaf: raw gold ~ two-thirds of manufactured article), while in others labour considerably exceeds material (e.g., silver-leaf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete retail examples: a book of 25 leaves of gold sold for 1s.6d; a book of 50 leaves of silver covering >1000 square inches sold for 1s.3d, illustrating differing labour/material proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size-dependent labour/material ratio (Venetian gold chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: In fine Venetian gold chains the relative influence of labour and material varies with size: the smallest chains can have labour value many times the gold; as size increases, material value rises and labour proportion falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabled data (1828) show sizes numbered 0..24 with weights, links, and prices; e.g., chain numbered 0 and 24 are same price though latter contains 22 times the gold — smallest chains are so difficult that workers cannot do long periods, producing very high labour cost relative to material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical ratios of raw material to manufactured value (Villefosse data)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given value of raw material (1£), its manufactured forms vary hugely in value — e.g., silk goods £2.37, broad cloth £2.15, copper woven into metallic cloth £52.23, needles 17.33–70.85, bracelets/buttons 147.00, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive tabulated French 1825 data list raw material worth 1£ and the manufactured articles' resulting values (silk, woollens, linen, cotton, lead, copper, tin, quicksilver, arsenic, cast iron, bar iron, steel, tinned iron, wire, etc.), illustrating the wide range of labour-augmentation factors across industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour: time required for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The time to acquire any art depends on the difficulty of its execution and the number of distinct processes; dividing labour confines attention to one operation and reduces the time unprofitably consumed at the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization allows apprentices to learn faster and to make better terms; restricting to one operation diminishes wasted training time and brings earlier productive contribution, which increases supply of labourers and tends to lower wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waste of material in learning is invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain quantity of material will be consumed unprofitably or spoiled by every person who learns an art; whether one man learns all processes or many people separately learn several processes, the total waste remains the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, with respect to material waste during learning, the division of labour neither increases nor diminishes the price of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of time from changing occupations and tool adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is lost in changing from one occupation to another because muscles and attention need adaptation; many tools require delicate adjustment, making changeovers costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization saves this switching cost. Example: complex tools (sliding-rest, dividing and drilling-engine) require substantial adjustment, so in large manufactories it's economical to keep machines permanently for one kind of work (e.g., one lathe making cylinders, another facing surfaces, another cutting wheels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill acquired by repetition (piece-work effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant repetition of the same process produces excellence and rapidity in that department not possessed by one person executing many processes; piece-work payment further increases rapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nail-making — a specialist can make over 2,300 nails/day versus 800–1,000 for a general smith; a Bank of England clerk signed his name 5,300 times in eleven hours. Although large initially, this advantage diminishes as overall experience accumulates over years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour encourages the contrivance of improved tools and machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: When each process becomes the sole occupation of an individual, improvements in tools or their use are more likely to be discovered, and such improvements are often the first step towards machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fixing the cutting-tool angle suggests a sliding-rest; mounting a chisel in a frame suggests the carpenter's plane; regularizing hammer blows suggests mechanical mounting — small tool improvements naturally progress toward machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining tools into machines requires mechanical education and drawing skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Union of many simple tools actuated by one power constitutes a machine; making such combinations successfully requires extensive knowledge of machinery and the power of making mechanical drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operative workmen are often best at contriving simple tool improvements, but combining many processes into a machine needs broader mechanical education; historical failures in early manufactures owed partly to absence of these skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master can procure precise mixtures of skill and strength via division
rubrics_metrics.description: By dividing work into different processes requiring different degrees of skill and force, a master can purchase exactly that precise quantity of each which is necessary for each process; a single workman would need both the skill for the hardest and strength for the most laborious operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies much of the economy resulting from division of labour and explains part of the cheapness of manufactured articles beyond dexterity, time saved, and machinery invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing organization: detailed sequential operations and task allocation (pin-making example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacture should be decomposed into specific successive operations (example: pin-making: wire-drawing; straightening; pointing; twisting and cutting heads; heading; tinning; papering) with different tasks allocated to men, women, children, and paid at piece or daily rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pin-making description gives operational details and rates (e.g., wire-drawers ~30–36 lb/day at five farthings per lb; pointers 34–36.5 lb/day earning 6s.6d total; head-fixing operators may do 10–20k pins/day paid 1s.6d per 20k; tinner earns ~9s/day less assistant cost). Use of gauges, mills, dies, annealing and pickling processes, and specific workplace ergonomics are illustrated as part of organizing production efficiently.
